items.subject: VR
items.prompt: RESOLUTE most nearly means:
items.explanation: resolute: determined, steadfast, unwavering — She remained resolute even after the first experiment failed.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Careless means not taking care or attention; being resolute is about holding firm, which is not the same thing at all.
why.C: Cheerful means happy and in good spirits, but resolute is about standing firm, and you can stand firm feeling anything but cheerful.
why.D: Doubtful means unsure and full of questions, which is the opposite of resolute — someone resolute has made up her mind.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: SANCTUARY most nearly means:
items.explanation: sanctuary: a shelter, refuge or safe place — The injured birds were taken to a wildlife sanctuary.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A rule tells you what you may or may not do, but a sanctuary is a place you go to be safe.
why.B: A punishment is something unpleasant given to you for doing wrong, but a sanctuary is the opposite — somewhere you are kept safe.
why.D: An argument is a disagreement in words, and a sanctuary is a safe place; the birds are being kept safe, not argued with.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: STIFLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: stifle: suppress, smother, hold back — She tried to stifle a laugh during the serious presentation.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Reveal means to show something that was hidden, but stifling a laugh means holding it in, which is the opposite.
why.B: Encourage means to urge something on and help it grow, but to stifle is to press it down instead.
why.C: Expand means to make something bigger or spread it out, but stifling is smothering something so that it gets no bigger.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: SUBORDINATE most nearly means:
items.explanation: subordinate: lower-ranking, secondary; or to place something below — The assistant held a subordinate position in the organization.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Equal means at the same level as someone else, but a subordinate is below someone in rank, which is a different relationship.
why.B: Superior describes the one above, the boss rather than the helper, but a subordinate is the one lower down.
why.D: Temporary means lasting only a short time, which is about how long something goes on, not about rank.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: TANGIBLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: tangible: concrete, touchable, real — The project produced tangible results that everyone could measure.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Secret means deliberately kept from other people, but tangible is about whether a thing is solid enough to touch.
why.B: Imaginary means existing only in the mind, which is the opposite of tangible; tangible results are real ones everyone could measure.
why.D: Distant means far off in space or time, but tangible is about whether you could touch a thing at all.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: TREACHEROUS most nearly means:
items.explanation: treacherous: dangerous, deceptive, disloyal — The icy mountain path was treacherous after the storm.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Ordinary means usual and nothing special, but treacherous is a warning that something could harm you, which is far stronger.
why.C: Quiet is about how much noise something makes, but treacherous is about danger, and an icy path can be noiseless and deadly.
why.D: Safe means free from danger, which is the exact opposite of treacherous.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: WHIMSICAL most nearly means:
items.explanation: whimsical: playful and fanciful, quirky — The illustrator filled the page with whimsical animals wearing tiny hats.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Gloomy means dark and low-spirited, which is the opposite of the light, playful feeling whimsical describes.
why.C: Practical means sensible and useful in real life, while whimsical means following your own fancy without worrying about being sensible.
why.D: Strict means keeping firmly to rules, but whimsical means letting your imagination wander wherever it likes.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: WANE most nearly means:
items.explanation: wane: decrease, diminish, fade — Her excitement began to wane after several hours of waiting.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Shine means to give off light, and although the moon does wane, waning means it is growing smaller, not glowing.
why.B: To vanish instantly is to be gone all at once, but waning is gradual — her excitement faded slowly, not in a blink.
why.C: Grow means to get larger, which is the opposite of wane; the moon waxes when it grows and wanes when it shrinks.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: CONSPICUOUS most nearly means:
items.explanation: conspicuous: noticeable, obvious, easy to pick out — Jo's bright red hair was conspicuous among the other girls.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Stubborn means refusing to change your mind, which is about someone's will, while conspicuous is about being easy to notice.
why.C: Careful means taking trouble to avoid mistakes, which says nothing about whether people notice you; conspicuous means you stand out.
why.D: Hidden means out of sight, the opposite of conspicuous — Jo's bright red hair was the thing everybody spotted.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ERADICATE most nearly means:
items.explanation: eradicate: eliminate, wipe out completely — Jo wished she could eradicate her quick temper, but she knew it was part of her.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Postpone means to put something off until later, so it still exists; eradicating something means getting rid of it completely.
why.C: Weaken means to make something less strong while it still remains, but eradicate is total — wiping the thing out altogether.
why.D: Imitate means to act out how something else looks or behaves, but eradicate is about destroying a thing completely.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The committee reached a ______ decision; every member agreed.
items.explanation: Unanimous means agreed by everyone, which is what “every member agreed” says; a tentative, private or random decision tells you nothing about agreement.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Tentative means not yet settled, only tried out for now — but the sentence says every member agreed, which is settled.
why.B: Private means kept from other people, which is about who was told, not about everyone agreeing.
why.C: Random means chosen by chance for no reason, but a decision every member agreed on was not left to chance.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Because the path crossed loose rocks and steep cliffs, hikers called it ______.
items.explanation: Treacherous means dangerous and not to be trusted, which is what loose rocks and steep cliffs make a path; rural, stable and spacious describe where it is or how wide it is, not the danger.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Rural means out in the countryside away from towns, which tells you where a path is, not how dangerous it is.
why.B: Stable means steady and firmly fixed, but loose rocks are the opposite of steady, so this path is anything but stable.
why.D: Spacious means having plenty of room, but loose rocks and steep cliffs make a path dangerous, not roomy.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: She tried to ______ her laughter during the serious ceremony.
items.explanation: To stifle is to hold something back, which is what you do with laughter in a serious ceremony; you cannot unite, retrieve or cultivate a laugh.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Unite means to join separate things into one, but there is only one laugh here, and she needs to hold it back.
why.C: Retrieve means to fetch something back that has gone, but laughter at a serious ceremony needs holding in, not fetching.
why.D: Cultivate means to grow something carefully, like a garden or a skill, which is the opposite of what laughter needs here.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The old church served as a ______ for families during the storm.
items.explanation: A sanctuary is a safe place to shelter in, which is what families need during a storm; a frontier, a spectator and a resolution are not places of safety.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A frontier is the far edge of settled land, a border region, not a building families could crowd into during a storm.
why.C: A spectator is a person who watches something happen, but the church in the sentence is a place, not a person.
why.D: A resolution is a firm decision to do something, or the settling of a problem, and neither is somewhere you can go.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: His confidence began to ______ after repeated failures.
items.explanation: To wane is to fade and grow less, which is what repeated failures do to confidence; to unify, restore or tower would mean it grew or held steady.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Unify means to join separate things into one, but repeated failures make confidence fade away, not come together.
why.B: Restore means to bring something back to the way it was, so his confidence would be returning, not slipping away.
why.C: To tower is to rise up high above everything around, which would mean his confidence grew after failing — the opposite.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The detective remained ______ about the suspect's story because several details did not match.
items.explanation: Dubious means doubtful, which is how details that do not match leave you; resolute, contented and jovial describe someone those details had not troubled.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A resolute person has stopped wondering, but details that do not match are exactly what leave the detective wondering.
why.B: Contented means quite happy with how things are, which is not how a story full of mismatched details leaves you.
why.D: Jovial means full of jokes and laughter, but the detective's trouble is that he does not believe the story.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: A signed receipt is ______ evidence that a payment was made.
items.explanation: Tangible means solid and touchable, which a signed receipt is; subjective, whimsical and remote all suggest evidence you cannot hold.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Subjective means it depends on how a person feels, but a signed receipt is proof that anyone can check.
why.B: Whimsical means full of odd little flights of imagination, which is not a quality that evidence can have.
why.C: Remote means far away, but a signed receipt is right there in your hand.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The new law expanded ______ by giving more citizens the right to vote.
items.explanation: Suffrage is the right to vote, which is exactly what the law gave more citizens; authority, patriotism and legislation are not that right.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Authority means the power to give orders and be obeyed, which is not the same as the right to vote.
why.C: Patriotism means love of your country, and a law cannot hand out a feeling the way it hands out the vote.
why.D: Legislation means laws, or the making of them — the new law is itself legislation, so it is doing the expanding.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Even though she was small, the ______ puppy barked boldly at the much larger dog.
items.explanation: Feisty means spirited and ready to stand up to anything, which is what barking boldly at a much larger dog is; sluggish, somber and aloof would all keep the puppy quiet.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Sluggish means slow and lacking energy, but barking boldly at a much larger dog takes plenty of energy.
why.C: Somber means serious and gloomy, a quiet and heavy mood, and this puppy is anything but quiet.
why.D: An aloof animal holds itself back and stays out of things, but this puppy is squaring up to the bigger dog.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: After the rival team played a dirty trick, the captain refused to ______ and instead reported it.
items.explanation: To retaliate is to pay a wrong back with a wrong, which is what the captain refused to do and reported instead; to retrieve, cultivate or reminisce is no answer to a dirty trick.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: You retrieve a ball or a dropped glove; a dirty trick is not something the captain could go and fetch back.
why.C: Cultivate means to grow or build something up slowly and carefully, which is no answer to a trick played in a moment.
why.D: Reminisce means to look back on the past and enjoy remembering it, but this trick has only just happened.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: PAINSTAKING most nearly means:
items.explanation: painstaking: meticulous, done slowly and with great care — The model ship was painstaking work, every rope tied by hand.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Hurried means done fast and under pressure, but painstaking work is slow, because taking that much care takes time.
why.C: Cheerful means in good spirits, which describes a mood, while painstaking describes how much care goes into the work.
why.D: Careless means done without attention, the exact opposite of painstaking — the word has 'pains' in it because you take pains.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ALOOF most nearly means:
items.explanation: aloof: distant and cool, keeping apart from other people — The new cat stayed aloof for a week before she would sit near anyone.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Generous means willing to give freely, but aloof is about keeping your distance from people, not about what you give.
why.C: Excited means full of eager, lively feeling, which is the opposite of the cool, unbothered manner that aloof describes.
why.D: Loyal describes someone who sticks by her friends; aloof is about keeping your distance, which is a different thing to measure.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: INEVITABLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: inevitable: certain to happen, impossible to avoid — With the clouds piling up, rain felt inevitable.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Hidden means out of sight, but inevitable is about whether a thing will happen, not whether you can see it coming.
why.B: Avoidable means you can find a way round it, which is the exact opposite of inevitable.
why.C: Optional means it is up to you, and nobody gets a choice about something inevitable.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: REMORSE most nearly means:
items.explanation: remorse: deep regret for something you have done — He felt remorse the moment he saw her face.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Pride is the warm feeling of being pleased with something you have done, while remorse is wishing you had not done it.
why.B: Confusion means not understanding what is going on, but someone feeling remorse understands only too well what they did.
why.D: A celebration is a happy marking of something good, the opposite of the sorry, regretful feeling remorse describes.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: DWINDLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: dwindle: shrink gradually, get smaller and smaller — The crowd began to dwindle once the rain started.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: To burst suddenly is to happen all at once, but dwindling is slow — the crowd thinned out little by little.
why.C: Repeat means to happen again, which is about how often something occurs, not about it getting smaller the way dwindle does.
why.D: Gather means to come together and build up, the opposite of dwindle — a crowd that dwindles is melting away.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: PROVOKE most nearly means:
items.explanation: provoke: incite, stir up, deliberately cause a reaction — Do not provoke the dog while it is eating.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Calm means to settle someone down and quieten them, which is the opposite of provoking them into a reaction.
why.C: Repair means to mend something broken, but provoking is about stirring a person or an animal up, not fixing anything.
why.D: Conceal means to keep a thing out of sight, but provoking is done openly, on purpose, to get a reaction.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: TERSE most nearly means:
items.explanation: terse: brief and to the point, sometimes curt — His terse reply was a single word: no.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Poetic means like poetry — full of imagery and careful rhythm — while terse means using as few words as possible, which is a different thing entirely.
why.B: Friendly means warm and kind toward people; terse is about how few words someone uses, and a terse reply is often not warm at all.
why.C: Elaborate means worked out in lots of detail with much added; terse means stripped down to almost nothing, so this is the opposite.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: RETRIEVE most nearly means:
items.explanation: retrieve: recover, fetch something back — The dog was trained to retrieve the ball and drop it at her feet.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Estimate means to make a careful guess at a number or amount; retrieving is going and getting something back, not guessing anything.
why.C: Divide means to split something into parts; retrieve is about bringing one thing back whole.
why.D: Abandon means to leave something behind for good, which is the opposite of going back to retrieve it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The family practiced strict ______, repairing clothes rather than buying new ones.
items.explanation: Economy here means careful thrift, which is what repairing clothes rather than buying new ones is; volume, whim and prestige have nothing to do with spending less.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Volume can mean how loud a sound is, or how much space something takes up, and it has other senses besides — none of them about spending less money.
why.C: A whim is a sudden idea you act on without thinking it through; mending clothes instead of buying new ones is a careful, steady habit, not a whim.
why.D: Prestige means the respect and admiration that something impressive attracts; this family is being thrifty, not trying to impress anyone.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: She used great ______ and did not reveal the surprise party.
items.explanation: Discretion is knowing what not to say, which is what keeping a surprise party quiet takes; a grievance, fatigue and turmoil are not kinds of judgment.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A grievance is a complaint you carry about something that was done to you; keeping a surprise quiet is not a complaint about anything.
why.B: Fatigue means great tiredness; being tired is not what keeps a secret safe.
why.D: Turmoil means a state of confusion and upheaval; saying nothing until the right moment is the steady opposite of that.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Several students ______ the speaker's claim and asked for evidence.
items.explanation: To dispute a claim is to challenge it, which is what asking for evidence does; to revere, cultivate or hoist a claim is not to question it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Revered means deeply respected, almost worshipped; asking for evidence is doubting the claim rather than honouring it.
why.C: Cultivated means grown or carefully developed, the way you cultivate a garden; you cannot cultivate a claim by demanding proof of it.
why.D: Hoisted means lifted or raised up, usually with ropes — you hoist a flag or a sail, not an argument.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The teacher gave ______ criticism that showed exactly how the essay could improve.
items.explanation: Constructive criticism is meant to help you improve, which is what showing exactly how the essay could get better does; hostile, ominous and trite criticism would not.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Hostile criticism comes at you like an attack; this criticism showed exactly how to make the essay better, which is help instead.
why.B: Ominous is how a black sky feels before a storm; advice on improving an essay is not a warning of trouble ahead.
why.D: Trite means dull and overused from being said too many times; these comments were specific to this essay, which is the opposite of trite.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: At the end of camp, the students had to ______ the temporary stage and pack away the pieces.
items.explanation: To dismantle is to take something apart piece by piece, which is what packing a temporary stage away means; to render, proclaim or reinforce it would leave it standing.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Render can mean to make something become a certain way — render it useless — but taking a thing apart is not one of its meanings.
why.B: Proclaim means to announce something publicly and officially; announcing the stage would not get it packed into boxes.
why.C: Reinforce means to make something stronger; that would keep the stage standing, and camp is over.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: A sudden crash in the hallway caused a loud ______ outside the classroom.
items.explanation: A commotion is a noisy disturbance, which is what a sudden crash causes; tranquility is its opposite, and leisure and consensus are not noises at all.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Tranquility means calm and quietness; a sudden crash destroys tranquility rather than causing it.
why.B: Leisure means free time when you have nothing you must do; it is not a sound, so it cannot be loud.
why.C: A consensus is something a group arrives at, not a sound; a crash in a hallway makes noise, and noise is not what consensus describes.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: As the rain became heavier, the crowd began to ______ until only a few people remained.
items.explanation: To dwindle is to get smaller and smaller, which is what a crowd does until only a few remain; to prosper, provoke or accumulate would mean it grew.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Prosper means to thrive and do well, usually in money or health; a crowd shrinking in the rain is not thriving.
why.C: You provoke someone by doing something that makes them react; nobody is being provoked here, the crowd is simply getting smaller.
why.D: Accumulate means to build up and grow in amount; the sentence says only a few people remained, so the crowd went the other way.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The old mansion seemed to ______ over the village from the top of the hill.
items.explanation: To loom is to rise over something largely and a little threateningly, which is what a mansion on a hilltop does over a village; to nestle is to settle snugly, and to recoil or wane is to draw back or fade.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Nestle means to settle in snugly and low, the way a cottage nestles in a valley; this mansion stands high on a hilltop above the village.
why.B: Recoil means to jerk back suddenly, usually out of fear or disgust; a building cannot draw back from anything.
why.D: Wane is what the moon does between full and a thin sliver; the mansion is standing over the village, not thinning away.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The students decided to ______ the store after learning about its unfair policy.
items.explanation: To boycott is to refuse to use a business as a protest, which is what an unfair policy provokes; to commend, consent or grant would be to approve of it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Commend means to praise someone for doing well; the policy was unfair, so the students are protesting rather than praising.
why.C: To consent is to say yes to something; the students disagreed with the policy, so saying yes is the opposite of what they did.
why.D: To grant something is to hand it over when you are the one who gets to decide; refusing to use a shop is not handing it anything.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: IMPLY most nearly means:
items.explanation: imply: suggest something without saying it outright — Her raised eyebrow seemed to imply she did not believe him. A speaker implies; a listener infers.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Deny means to say that something is not true; implying is quietly hinting at something without saying it at all, which is a different act altogether.
why.C: Copy means to make something the same as something else; imply is about hinting at a meaning, and nothing is being repeated.
why.D: Prove means to show beyond doubt that something is true; implying only hints, and a hint is far weaker than proof.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: INFER most nearly means:
items.explanation: infer: conclude something from the clues you are given — From the muddy boots she could infer that he had walked home. A speaker implies; a listener infers.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Repeat means to say or do something over again; inferring works out something new from the clues instead.
why.C: Observe means to notice something with your senses, and it is the step just before inferring, not the same step.
why.D: Question means to ask about something or to doubt it; inferring is arriving at an answer from the clues, not raising a doubt about them.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: OBJECTIVE most nearly means:
items.explanation: objective: unbiased, based on facts rather than feelings — A thermometer gives an objective answer; “too hot” is an opinion.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Secret means hidden or kept from other people; being objective is about judging by facts rather than feelings, and has nothing to do with hiding anything.
why.B: Careless means not taking care or paying attention; staying objective usually takes more care, not less.
why.C: Emotional means led by feelings, which is exactly what objective is not — objective means going by the facts instead.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: SUBJECTIVE most nearly means:
items.explanation: subjective: based on personal opinion or feeling — Which flavour is best is subjective; how many scoops there are is not.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Something able to be measured comes out the same for everyone who checks it; a subjective view is one person's own, and no ruler can settle that.
why.C: Beyond all doubt means proven and certain; a subjective view is one person's opinion, and other people can reasonably disagree with it.
why.D: Public means open to everyone or belonging to everyone; subjective is about whose feelings a judgment comes from, not about who is allowed to see it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: RIGOROUS most nearly means:
items.explanation: rigorous: thorough and demanding, leaving nothing out — The school had rigorous training that ran every morning before lessons.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Easily bent describes a flexible material; rigorous is about work — training or testing that is thorough and demands a lot of you.
why.B: Relaxed and informal means easy-going, with few rules; rigorous means the opposite, demanding and leaving nothing out.
why.D: Motionless describes something frozen in place; rigorous says how demanding and thorough something is, not whether anything holds still.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: RIGID most nearly means:
items.explanation: rigid: inflexible, not bending — The rules were rigid: no exceptions for anyone.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Careful means paying close attention so as not to make a mistake; being careful still lets you bend when it makes sense.
why.B: Uncertain means not sure; rigid rules are the opposite of unsure — they simply refuse to bend.
why.C: Playful means full of fun and games; rigid means stiff and unbending, which is close to its opposite.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: STATIONARY most nearly means:
items.explanation: stationary: not moving, standing still — The car was stationary at the lights. Stationery with an e is paper and pens.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Something easily moved is portable or mobile — stationary is its opposite, standing still in one place.
why.C: Lasting a short time is what temporary means; stationary is about not moving, not about how long something lasts.
why.D: Paper and pens are stationery, spelt with an e near the end; stationary with an a means standing still.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: STATIC most nearly means:
items.explanation: static: unchanging, motionless — The population remained static for several years.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Polite means having good manners; static means staying the same, which says nothing about how a person behaves.
why.B: Crowded means full of people; a static population is one that is not changing in size, which is not the same as being large.
why.C: Dangerous means likely to cause harm; static simply means unchanging or still, and staying the same is not risky.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: SUBORDINATE most nearly means:
items.explanation: subordinate: lower-ranking, secondary; or to place something below — The assistant held a subordinate position in the organization.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Independent means not under anyone else's control; a subordinate is exactly the opposite, someone working under a higher rank.
why.B: Celebrated means famous and widely praised; a subordinate position is a lower one, whether or not anybody praises the person in it.
why.D: Unanimous has to do with agreement; subordinate is about rank, about being placed below someone.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: INFERIOR most nearly means:
items.explanation: inferior: lower in quality or rank than something else — The cheaper paint was clearly inferior: it peeled within a month.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: More expensive is about price, not worth — a cheap thing can be well made, and an expensive one can still be lower in quality.
why.C: Less visible would mean harder to see; inferior means lower in quality or rank, not tucked out of sight.
why.D: Older is about age; something old can still be excellent, while inferior means lower in quality or rank than something else.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: From the wet footprints leading to the kitchen, Maya could ______ that someone had entered through the back door.
items.explanation: To infer is to work something out from the clues, which is what wet footprints let Maya do. Imply is the other side of the same act: the footprints imply it, and Maya infers it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: You conserve water or energy by using as little of it as you can; wet footprints do not let Maya conserve anything, they let her work something out.
why.C: Imply means to hint at something, and here it is the footprints doing the hinting — Maya is reading the hint, not giving one.
why.D: Restore means to put something back the way it was, like restoring an old painting; Maya is working out what happened, not repairing anything.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The author never says the character is afraid, but the shaking hands and short breaths ______ fear.
items.explanation: To imply is to suggest something without saying it, which is what shaking hands and short breaths do while the author stays silent. A reader concludes, but only the details imply.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Conclude means to decide something after thinking it through, which is what a reader does; the shaking hands are only details, and details cannot decide anything.
why.C: Retrieve is what you do when you go back for something you left behind; the shaking hands and short breaths are pointing at fear, not going to get anything.
why.D: Attain is what you do when you finally get to something you have been working towards; these details are hinting at fear, not getting anywhere.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The watchmaker examined the ______ gears, each tiny part fitting precisely with the next.
items.explanation: Intricate means made of many small parts fitting together, which is what tiny gears meshing precisely are; remote, subjective and static say nothing about detail.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Remote means far away or out of the way; the gears are right under the watchmaker's eyes, and remote says nothing about how finely made they are.
why.B: Subjective means it depends on who is judging; these gears are real objects, and the sentence describes how they are built, not how anyone feels about them.
why.C: Static describes something that stays put; gears are built to turn, and in any case static says nothing about all those tiny parts fitting together.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The report used measurable data and tried to remain ______ rather than emotional.
items.explanation: Objective means based on facts rather than feelings, which is what measurable data and “rather than emotional” both ask for; conspicuous, rigid and literal are not the opposite of emotional.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Conspicuous is what a bright red coat in a grey crowd is; a report can be conspicuous and still be full of feeling, so that is not the opposite of emotional.
why.C: Rigid describes rules that allow no exceptions; sticking rigidly to rules does not stop a report being emotional, which is what the sentence rules out.
why.D: Literal means taking words at their exact meaning, with no metaphor or exaggeration; that is about how language is read, not about keeping feelings out of a report.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: After a long discussion, the committee reached a ______ that the event should be postponed.
items.explanation: A consensus is a general agreement reached by a group, which is what a committee comes to after a long discussion; content, capital and decline are not agreements.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Content can describe someone who is happy with what they have, or the things inside a box; neither one is an agreement.
why.B: Capital can mean a country's main city, or a large letter, among other things; none of its meanings is something a committee arrives at.
why.C: A decline is a drop or a fall, the way sales decline; the committee agreed on something, and an agreement is not a drop.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The fall school ______ begins in September.
items.explanation: A term is a part of the school year, which is what begins in September; stock, volume and compact are not stretches of time.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Stock means a supply of goods kept ready, like a shop's stock of notebooks; a supply is a pile of things, not a stretch of the school year.
why.B: Volume is not a stretch of time, so nothing about a volume can begin in September — the parts of a school year have names like term and semester.
why.D: A compact is a formal agreement between people, and as an adjective compact means packed small and neat; neither one is a stretch of the school year.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Please turn down the ______; the music is too loud.
items.explanation: Volume here means loudness, which is the thing you turn down when music is too loud; a prompt, content and capital cannot be turned down.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: A prompt is a cue or reminder telling you what to say or do next, and a cue is not something on a music player you can turn down.
why.C: Content means what is inside something, like the content of a song or a book, and turning down what is inside would not make the music quieter — said the other way round, con-TENT, it is a different word altogether.
why.D: Capital means a country's main city, or a big letter at the start of a name; neither one has a loudness you can turn down.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: She sent a ______ reply within five minutes.
items.explanation: Prompt means quick, done without delay, which is what a reply within five minutes is; rigid, static and remote describe something else entirely.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Rigid means stiff and unbending, like a rigid ruler or a rigid rule; it says nothing about how soon the reply arrived.
why.B: Static means staying the same, not moving or changing; a reply sent within five minutes is about speed, not about standing still.
why.D: Remote means far away, like a remote island; the sentence tells you how soon she replied, not how far off she was.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The bus remained ______ at the curb while passengers boarded.
items.explanation: Stationary means not moving, which is what a bus at the curb is while passengers board; stable means steady, rigorous means demanding, elaborate means complicated.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A bus can be perfectly stable — steady and not tipping — while it drives along, and this one is not moving at all.
why.B: Rigorous means strict and thorough, like rigorous training or a rigorous check; it describes how carefully something is done, not a bus waiting at a curb.
why.D: Elaborate means worked out in great detail with many parts, like an elaborate costume; a bus holding still is not being called complicated.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Despite small changes in the weather, the patient's condition remained ______.
items.explanation: Stable means steady, holding safely where it is, which is what a condition that survives small changes does; static would mean nothing changed at all, and subjective and inferior are not about steadiness.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Subjective means based on personal feelings rather than facts, like a subjective opinion; a patient's condition is a fact about her health, not an opinion.
why.D: Inferior means lower in rank or worse in quality, and it compares one thing with another; the sentence is saying the condition held its ground, not that it was worse than something else.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ADMONISH most nearly means:
items.explanation: admonish: warn or scold, gently but firmly — The librarian admonished them for running between the shelves.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Paying no attention to something is ignoring it, and admonishing is the opposite — it means speaking up and telling the person off.
why.C: Praising warmly is telling someone they did well; admonishing points the other way, at something they should not have done.
why.D: Confusing someone means muddling them so they cannot follow; someone who is admonished is not muddled at all — they know exactly what they are being told off for.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ATTAIN most nearly means:
items.explanation: attain: achieve, reach something you aimed for — She trained all year to attain the qualifying time.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Avoiding something means keeping away from it; attaining is the opposite move — you go after a thing and reach it.
why.C: Measuring means finding out how big or how much something is; attaining a goal means reaching it, not sizing it up.
why.D: Lending means letting someone borrow something for a while; attaining is about getting hold of something yourself.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: AVERT most nearly means:
items.explanation: avert: prevent something bad, or turn away — He swerved and averted an accident by inches.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Collecting means gathering things together; averting is about stopping something bad before it can happen.
why.C: Describing means saying in words what something is like; averting a disaster keeps it from happening at all, which is doing rather than telling.
why.D: Celebrating means marking a happy occasion; the things you avert are the unhappy ones — you turn them away.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: CONCISE most nearly means:
items.explanation: concise: brief and clear, saying it in few words — Her concise answer took one sentence and left nothing out.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Being not at all sure means being uncertain or doubtful; concise is about the length of what you say, not how confident you are saying it.
why.C: Angry is a feeling; concise describes how something is written or said — in few clear words — and a concise answer can be given in any mood.
why.D: Using too many words is being wordy or long-winded, which is the exact opposite of concise.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: CONSERVE most nearly means:
items.explanation: conserve: save and protect something so it lasts — They conserve water in summer by watering the garden at night.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Dividing means splitting something into parts; conserving is about making something last, not sharing it out.
why.B: Spending quickly means using something up fast, which is the opposite of conserving it.
why.C: Criticizing means pointing out what is wrong with something; conserving is looking after a thing, not judging it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: DISSENT most nearly means:
items.explanation: dissent: disagreement, especially with an official view — One judge wrote a dissent explaining why she disagreed.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Calmness means being quiet and untroubled; dissent is the opposite mood — making it known that you disagree.
why.B: Wealth means having a great deal of money, and dissent has nothing to do with riches.
why.C: The word for permission is consent, which looks almost the same as dissent but means the opposite: agreeing rather than disagreeing.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ELUDE most nearly means:
items.explanation: elude: escape or avoid, slip out of reach — The fox eluded the dogs by doubling back along the stream.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Giving help to someone is coming to their aid; eluding is getting away from whoever is after you.
why.C: Explaining something in detail until it is clear is to elucidate, a word that starts like elude; eluding itself is slipping out of reach.
why.D: Repairing means fixing something broken; eluding is escaping, and nothing is being mended.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ELIGIBLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: eligible: qualified, allowed to take part — Only pupils in the top year were eligible to enter.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Doubtful means unsure or unlikely; eligible is not about how likely something is, but about whether you are allowed to take part.
why.C: Hidden means out of sight; the look-alike to watch for is illegible, which means too messy to read, while eligible means allowed to join in.
why.D: Famous means widely known; being eligible says nothing about fame, only that you meet the conditions.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: ESTEEM most nearly means:
items.explanation: esteem: respect, a high opinion of someone — The old teacher was held in great esteem by everyone who had learned from her.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Confusion means being muddled and not understanding; esteem is an opinion you hold about a person — a high one.
why.B: Anger means being cross with someone; esteem is the warm opposite, thinking highly of them.
why.C: Fear means being afraid of someone; you can hold a person in great esteem without being frightened of them at all.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: EVOKE most nearly means:
items.explanation: evoke: bring to mind, call up a feeling or a memory — The smell of the kitchen evoked her grandmother's house.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Making something smaller is reducing or shrinking it; evoking calls up a memory or a feeling, and nothing changes size.
why.B: Removing something completely, such as canceling a rule or a license, is to revoke it — one letter from evoke, which instead brings a feeling or a memory to mind.
why.D: Delaying means putting something off until later; evoking happens at once, the way a smell brings a memory straight back.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The rope began to ______ after rubbing against the rough stone.
items.explanation: To fray is to wear into loose threads, which is what rubbing against rough stone does to a rope; a rope cannot attain, prosper or grant.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Attain means to achieve something you aimed for, and a rope has no goal to reach.
why.C: Prosper means to thrive and do well, the way a business or a garden does; a rope rubbing on stone is being damaged, not flourishing.
why.D: Grant means to give someone what they asked for; a rope gives nothing away — it wears into loose threads.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Her main ______ was that the new rule treated younger students unfairly.
items.explanation: A grievance is a complaint about unfair treatment, which is exactly what “treated younger students unfairly” describes; an expanse, consent and leeway are not complaints.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: An expanse is a wide open stretch of land, sea or sky; it names a space, not a complaint about a rule.
why.B: Consent means permission, saying yes to something, and she is objecting to the new rule rather than agreeing to it.
why.D: Leeway means a little room to move, some slack or extra time; room to move is not a complaint about a rule.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The crowd became ______ after the referee made the unpopular call.
items.explanation: Hostile means angry and unfriendly, which is what an unpopular call makes a crowd; fortunate, eligible and concise are not moods.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Fortunate means lucky, and a crowd annoyed by the referee is not being called lucky.
why.B: Eligible means allowed to take part, the way a player qualifies for a team; it says who may join in, not how a crowd feels.
why.C: Concise means saying something in few clear words; it describes writing or speech, not the mood of a crowd.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: He was completely ______ at repairing the bicycle and made the problem worse.
items.explanation: Inept means clumsy and unskilled, which is what making the problem worse shows; cordial, renowned and jovial say nothing about skill.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Cordial means warm and friendly in a polite way, and you can be perfectly friendly and still be hopeless at fixing a bicycle.
why.B: Renowned means famous, widely known — but being famous is not the same as being good at the job, and this sentence is about how badly he did it.
why.D: Jovial means cheerful and full of good humor; that is his mood, not his skill with a bicycle.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The teacher gave students some ______ in choosing their project topics.
items.explanation: Leeway is room to choose for yourself, which is what letting students pick their own topics gives; a fray, esteem and descent are not freedoms.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A fray is a fight or a scuffle, and to fray is to wear into loose threads; neither is something a teacher hands out with project topics.
why.B: Esteem means respect, a high opinion of someone; what the teacher is giving here is a choice, not her good opinion.
why.D: Descent means a way down, or the family you come from; going downhill is not the same as being given room to choose.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The hikers survived on a ______ supply of food until help arrived.
items.explanation: Meager means barely enough, which is what a supply you merely survive on is; ample is its opposite, and glorious and compact do not measure quantity.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Ample means plenty, more than enough; if the hikers had plenty of food, merely surviving on it would not be worth saying.
why.C: Glorious means splendid and wonderful; it praises the food rather than telling you how much of it there was.
why.D: Compact means packed neatly into a small space, and a compact supply could still be a large one; the sentence is about how little they had.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: A sudden storm ______ their plan to hold the concert outdoors.
items.explanation: To thwart is to stop a plan from happening, which is what a sudden storm does to an outdoor concert; to elude, cultivate or commend a plan is not to wreck it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: To elude is to slip out of reach of whoever is chasing you; a storm does not escape a plan, it wrecks it.
why.C: To cultivate is to grow something and look after it, like a garden or a friendship; a storm does not nurse a plan along.
why.D: To commend is to praise, and a storm cannot praise a plan — nor would praise have stopped the concert.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: In “The company raised more capital,” CAPITAL means:
items.explanation: capital: money or financial resources put into a business — The company raised more capital to open a second shop. Capital is also a capital city and a capital letter; the sentence around it tells you which one is meant.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A capital really is the carved top of a column, but a company raising capital is raising money, not carving stone.
why.B: A capital is a country's main city, which is a true meaning of the word; a company raises money, though, not cities.
why.C: The only place capital means punishment is the old legal phrase capital punishment; a company raising capital is raising money.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: In “Beth was content with the simple meal,” CONTENT means:
items.explanation: content: satisfied, happy with what you have — Beth was content with the simple meal. Said with the stress on the front, CON-tent, it means what is inside something.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: The information inside a book is its content, said CON-tent — but about a person, con-TENT means happy with what she has.
why.C: Crowded means packed full of people or things; the contents of a box can be crammed in, but a person who is content is simply satisfied.
why.D: Angry is close to the opposite: being content with a simple meal means being quite happy with it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: In “The volume of water in the tank increased,” VOLUME means:
items.explanation: volume: an amount or quantity of something — The volume of water in the tank increased. Volume is also loudness, and a single book out of a set; here it is how much there is.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Loudness is a real meaning of volume, the one on a music player, but water rising in a tank makes no sound; here volume is how much there is.
why.C: A volume is also one book out of a set, which is why libraries number them; a tank holds water, not books.
why.D: Volume never means a promise — the words for that are a vow or a pledge.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: In “Her ankle was still tender after the fall,” TENDER means:
items.explanation: tender: painful or sensitive to the touch — Her ankle was still tender after the fall. Tender also means gentle and kind, which is the meaning you meet far more often.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Nothing about tender means quick — tender meat is soft rather than tough, and a tender ankle is sore to touch.
why.C: You can tender your resignation, which means to offer it formally, but an ankle cannot offer anything; here tender means sore to touch.
why.D: Tender does mean kind and generous, and that is the meaning you meet most often, but an ankle is not being called kind — after a fall it is sore.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The unexpected compliment ______ her to keep working.
items.explanation: To prompt someone is to push them into acting, which is what an unexpected compliment did; declined, traced and stocked describe nothing about being spurred on.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Declined means turned something down or refused it politely; a compliment that kept her working pushed her on rather than refusing anything.
why.B: Traced means copied a picture by drawing over its lines; a compliment did not copy anything, it spurred her on.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The store ______ several kinds of art paper.
items.explanation: To stock is to keep goods ready for sale, which is what a store does with art paper; a store cannot charter, conflict or render paper.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Charters means hires a whole bus, boat or plane for one group's use; a shop might charter a van, but it cannot charter the paper on its shelves.
why.B: A conflict is a fight or a quarrel; sheets of paper sitting in a shop are not quarrelling with anything.
why.C: Renders can mean presents something in a particular form, the way an artist renders a drawing; a shop keeps its goods ready for sale rather than rendering them.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: One ______ of the agreement requires payment by Friday.
items.explanation: A term here is one condition of an agreement, which is what requires payment by Friday; capital, trace and volume are not conditions.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Capital means money used to run a business, or a country's chief city; neither is a condition written into an agreement.
why.B: A trace is a mark or sign that something has left behind, like footprints in snow; the conditions inside an agreement are not marks.
why.D: Volume means how loud a sound is, or the amount of space something fills; neither is a condition of an agreement.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: There was only a ______ of sugar left in the jar.
items.explanation: A trace is a tiny amount left behind, which is what “only a ______ of sugar” asks for; content, grant and charter are not quantities.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Content means satisfied and happy with what you have, and the contents of a jar are what is inside it; neither one names a tiny amount left over.
why.C: A grant is a sum of money given officially for a purpose, such as a grant to build a library; nobody gave out the sugar, there was simply a little of it left.
why.D: A charter is the hiring of a whole bus, boat or plane for one group; it is never an amount of something.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The volunteers agreed to ______ assistance after the storm.
items.explanation: To render assistance is to give it, which is what volunteers agreed to do after the storm; to exploit, decline or suspend assistance is to withhold it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Exploit means to use someone or something unfairly for your own gain; volunteers after a storm are giving help, not taking advantage.
why.C: Decline means to turn something down politely, so declining assistance would be refusing it — but the volunteers agreed to help.
why.D: Suspend means to hang something up, or to pause it for a time; pausing help is the opposite of what the volunteers agreed to do after a storm.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The principal decided to ______ permission for the field trip.
items.explanation: To grant is to give permission formally, which is what a principal does for a field trip; permission cannot be stocked, traced or conflicted.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Stock means to keep a supply of goods ready for sale; permission is not a thing kept on a shelf.
why.C: Trace means to copy a picture line by line through thin paper; a principal gives permission rather than tracing it.
why.D: A conflict is a fight or a quarrel; permission is something a principal hands out, not something that quarrels.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: A city ______ is a formal document describing the city's powers.
items.explanation: A charter is a formal document setting out powers, which is exactly what the sentence describes; discipline, a prompt and volume are not documents.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Discipline can mean keeping order in a class, or a branch of study such as history; neither one is a document.
why.B: Prompt means quick and on time, and a prompt is a short cue someone is given; neither is a written document.
why.C: Volume means how loud a sound is, or the amount of space something fills; a document setting out a city's powers is neither.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Finishing homework before playing games requires self-______.
items.explanation: Self-discipline is making yourself do the work first, which is what finishing homework before games takes; capital, content and trace are not habits of self-control.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Capital means money for running a business, or a country's chief city; neither has anything to do with making yourself do the work first.
why.B: Content means satisfied and happy with what you have — but being content with yourself is not the same as making yourself finish the homework before the games.
why.C: A trace is a faint mark or a tiny leftover amount; a mark left behind has nothing to do with controlling yourself.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: A dishonest employer may ______ workers by paying unfair wages.
items.explanation: To exploit people is to use them unfairly for your own gain, which is what unfair wages do; to charter, render or cultivate workers is not mistreatment.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Charter means to hire a whole bus, boat or plane for a group; that is nothing to do with how an employer treats workers.
why.C: Render means to give or deliver something, or to present it in a particular form; it does not describe treating people unfairly.
why.D: Cultivate means to grow plants and look after them, the way a gardener does; an employer paying unfair wages is not growing anything.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: She politely chose to ______ the invitation.
items.explanation: To decline is to refuse politely, which is what “politely chose to” points at; to suspend, grant or stock an invitation is not to turn it down.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Suspend means to stop something for a time, or to hang it up; a rule can be suspended, but an invitation is either accepted or turned down.
why.C: Grant means to give someone something they asked for; she was the one invited, so she was answering the invitation rather than handing it out.
why.D: Stock means to keep a supply of goods ready to sell; an invitation is not something kept on a shelf.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: A “remote possibility” is one that is:
items.explanation: remote: in this phrase, unlikely — a remote possibility is one that is barely possible. The everyday meaning is far away, and that is where this use comes from: a chance so distant you can hardly see it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Formal means official and following set rules; a remote possibility is about how likely something is, not about how official it is.
why.C: Nearby means close at hand; remote can mean far away, but in this phrase it is about how slim a chance is.
why.D: Dangerous means likely to cause harm; calling a possibility remote says only that it is barely likely, whether it would be good or bad.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The camera's ______ design made it easy to carry in a small bag.
items.explanation: Compact means small and neatly packed, which is what makes a camera easy to carry in a small bag; tender, remote and domestic say nothing about size.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Tender means gentle and kind, or soft and easy to chew; none of that would make a camera fit in a small bag.
why.B: Remote means far away, like a remote village or a remote control you press from across the room; none of that is about being small.
why.C: Domestic means to do with the home — domestic chores, a domestic cat; a camera used around the house could still be far too big for a small bag.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: In “domestic policy,” DOMESTIC most nearly means:
items.explanation: domestic: internal to one's own country — domestic policy is about home affairs rather than other nations. The same word also means “to do with the home”, which is why a cat that lives indoors is a domestic cat.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: "From another country" is what foreign means, and it is the opposite of domestic — domestic policy deals with matters inside the country itself.
why.B: Ancient means very old, from long ago; domestic says nothing about age.
why.D: "Kept very private" means hidden from others; a country's domestic policy is its public business at home, not a secret.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Good leaders try to ______ trust over time.
items.explanation: To cultivate is to build something up slowly, the way a plant is grown, which is what “over time” signals about trust; to decline, suspend or trace trust is not to grow it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Decline means to refuse politely, or to get gradually worse; leaders are building trust up, not turning it down or letting it fade.
why.C: Suspend means to halt something for a while; "over time" points to trust being grown steadily, not paused.
why.D: Trace means to copy a picture by drawing over its lines through thin paper; trust is grown over time, not copied.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The school may ______ a student for several days after a serious rule violation.
items.explanation: To suspend a student is to bar them from school for a time, which is what a serious violation leads to; to grant, exploit or render a student makes no sense.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Grant means to give something formally, such as permission or money; a school answering a serious rule-break is taking something away, not giving it.
why.B: Exploit means to use someone unfairly for your own gain; a school punishing a rule-break is not taking advantage of the student.
why.D: Render means to give or deliver something, or to present it in a particular form; it is not what a school does to a student for several days.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: If two witness statements CONFLICT, they:
items.explanation: conflict: to disagree or contradict each other — two accounts conflict when they cannot both be true. Said with the stress on the front, CON-flict, it is a noun meaning a fight or a dispute.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Lengthy just means long; two statements can conflict in one short sentence each, so length is not what the word is about.
why.B: Two statements that agree exactly tell the very same story; when statements conflict they clash, so they cannot both be true.
why.D: "Legally binding" means something the law will hold you to; whether two accounts clash has nothing to do with whether they bind anyone.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: AMPLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: ample: plentiful, more than enough — There was ample room for everyone to sit down.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Brief means lasting only a short time; ample is about there being plenty of something, so for time the two are near opposites.
why.B: Hostile means unfriendly and ready to fight; ample tells you how much of something there is, not how someone behaves.
why.D: Scarce means there is hardly any to be had, which is the exact opposite of having plenty.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: CORDIAL most nearly means:
items.explanation: cordial: warm and friendly, though polite rather than close — They exchanged cordial greetings at the gate.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: "Kept secret" means hidden from other people; a cordial greeting is out in the open and friendly.
why.B: Being careless means not paying attention to what you are doing; cordial is about warmth and politeness, which is a different thing entirely.
why.D: Severe means harsh and stern; that is close to the opposite of a cordial welcome.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: DRASTIC most nearly means:
items.explanation: drastic: extreme, severe, far beyond a small change — Cutting the budget in half was a drastic step.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Gradual means happening little by little; drastic is about how far a change goes, not how fast — a drastic cut is a severe one.
why.B: Doubtful means uncertain, not sure to happen; drastic is about how big and severe something is, not how likely.
why.C: Ordinary means usual and nothing special; drastic means going far beyond the usual.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: EXPANSE most nearly means:
items.explanation: expanse: a wide stretch of something open — A grey expanse of sea filled the window.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: "A large reward" is a prize for something you did; an expanse is a wide open stretch of land, sea or sky, and has nothing to do with payment.
why.C: "A formal complaint" is an objection made officially; an expanse is a stretch of open space, not something you say or write.
why.D: A mistake is something done wrong; an expanse is simply a wide open space, which is a completely different idea.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: FEROCIOUS most nearly means:
items.explanation: ferocious: fierce, savage, very violent — A ferocious wind tore the tiles off the roof.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Gentle means mild and careful; that is the opposite of ferocious.
why.B: Fair means just and even-handed (or light in colour); ferocious is about savage force, not about being fair.
why.D: Quiet means making little noise; a ferocious storm is usually loud, and in any case the word means fierce and violent rather than silent.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: She was ______ to catch the very last bus home.
items.explanation: Fortunate means lucky, favoured by chance, and catching the very last bus is luck.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Strict means insisting that rules be followed exactly; catching the very last bus is a matter of luck, not of rules.
why.C: Uncertain means not sure about something; she might have felt uncertain while waiting, but the sentence needs a word for how lucky she was to catch it.
why.D: Angry means cross or furious; catching the last bus home is good news, so the blank calls for a happier word.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: HASTY most nearly means:
items.explanation: hasty: hurried or rash, done too quickly to think — Jo regretted her hasty words the moment she saw Amy's hurt expression.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Stable means steady and unlikely to change or fall over; hasty is about doing something too quickly, which is a different idea altogether.
why.C: "Slow and careful" is the opposite of hasty — something hasty is done too fast to think it through.
why.D: "Used in ceremonies" is what ceremonial means; hasty is about speed, not about formal occasions.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: HOAX most nearly means:
items.explanation: hoax: a deception, a trick meant to be believed — The photograph of the monster turned out to be a hoax.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.C: A charter is the hiring of a whole plane, boat or bus for one group; that is not a trick played on people.
why.D: A remedy is a cure or a fix for a problem; a hoax creates a problem rather than solving one.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: HONORABLE most nearly means:
items.explanation: honorable: noble and upright, deserving respect — Returning the wallet untouched was the honorable thing to do.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: "Far away" is what remote means; honorable describes a person's character, not distance.
why.B: Weak means lacking strength; an honorable person may be strong or weak, because the word is about doing what is right.
why.C: "Hard to control" describes someone unruly, who will not do as they are told; honorable is about doing what is right, which is a different thing.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: INTACT most nearly means:
items.explanation: intact: undamaged, whole, with nothing missing — The parcel had been thrown about, but the vase inside was intact.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Broken means damaged or in pieces, which is the opposite of intact.
why.C: Hidden means out of sight; something can be intact in plain view, because intact is about being whole rather than about being seen.
why.D: Temporary means lasting only a short time; intact says nothing about how long something lasts, only that nothing is damaged or missing.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: JOVIAL most nearly means:
items.explanation: jovial: cheerful and good-humoured — Her uncle was a jovial man who laughed at his own jokes.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Stubborn means refusing to change your mind, which tells you nothing about a person's mood; jovial is about being cheerful and merry.
why.C: Solemn means serious and grave, the way you speak when something matters deeply, which is close to the opposite of jovial.
why.D: Formal means proper and following the polite rules, like a formal dinner; a jovial person is warm and laughing, and being correct is not the same as being merry.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: KNACK most nearly means:
items.explanation: knack: a talent, a handy skill picked up rather than taught — He had a knack for getting stubborn locks open.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: A warning is a message telling you trouble may be coming; a knack is something you are good at, not something you are told.
why.C: An obligation is something you are required to do whether you are good at it or not; a knack is an ability you happen to have.
why.D: An argument is a disagreement, or the reasons you give for your side of one; a knack is a skill.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: LOATHE most nearly means:
items.explanation: loathe: detest, hate strongly — She loathed the smell of boiled cabbage.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Admire means to look up to something and think well of it, which is the opposite of loathing it.
why.B: Copy means to make something the same as something else; loathing is a strong feeling of hate, not something you make.
why.C: Postpone means to put something off until later; loathe is about hating a thing, not about delaying it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: OMINOUS most nearly means:
items.explanation: ominous: threatening, a sign that something bad is coming — An ominous silence fell before the storm.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Spacious means having plenty of room, like a spacious hall; ominous is about a feeling of danger, not about size.
why.C: Ordinary means usual and nothing special; something ominous is the opposite, because it stands out as a sign that something bad is coming.
why.D: Playful means full of fun and games; ominous carries a sense of dread instead.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: PALTRY most nearly means:
items.explanation: paltry: meager or insignificant, far too small to matter — He was offered a paltry sum for a week's work.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Careful means paying close attention so you do not make mistakes; paltry is about how small an amount is, not about how carefully it was handled.
why.B: Full of energy describes someone lively and busy; paltry describes an amount so small it hardly counts.
why.D: Belonging to a king is what royal means; paltry describes an amount so small it is pitiful, the very opposite of anything grand.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: REFUGE most nearly means:
items.explanation: refuge: shelter or haven, a place safe from harm — They took refuge under the bridge until the hail stopped.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A complete failure is something that went wrong from start to finish; a refuge is a place, somewhere you go to be safe.
why.B: A law is a rule made and enforced by a government; refuge is about being sheltered from harm, not about rules.
why.C: A sharp insult is something unkind said to hurt; a refuge is a safe place, and there is nothing unkind about it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: REVOKE most nearly means:
items.explanation: revoke: cancel, take back something that was granted — The club revoked his membership after the third warning.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Celebrate means to mark a happy occasion; revoking something takes it away from someone, which is nobody's celebration.
why.B: Announce means to make something publicly known. Revoke sounds like invoke and provoke, but it means to withdraw something that was given rather than to declare it.
why.D: Combine means to join two things into one; revoke is about withdrawing something, not joining anything.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The engineer stopped to ______ the bridge for cracks before reopening it.
items.explanation: To inspect is to look over carefully, which is what checking a bridge for cracks is; to wander, reminisce or proclaim is not an examination.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Wander means to stroll about with no particular aim; looking for cracks in a bridge needs close attention, not aimless walking.
why.C: Reminisce means to think or talk fondly about the past; the engineer is checking the bridge now, not remembering it.
why.D: Proclaim means to announce something publicly and formally, which is not how anyone finds cracks in a bridge.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Stories and traditions passed down through generations are called ______.
items.explanation: Lore is the body of stories and traditions handed down, which is exactly what the sentence describes; stock, capital and discipline are not stories.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Stock can mean the family line a person comes from, which is close to handed-down stories but is about people, not tales.
why.B: Capital can mean a country's chief city, or a big letter at the start of a name, or a kind of money, but none of those is a set of traditions.
why.C: Discipline means keeping yourself in order and sticking to the rules; stories handed down through families are not a kind of order.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The students built a ______ stage from cardboard boxes and old curtains.
items.explanation: Makeshift means put together from whatever is to hand, which is what cardboard boxes and old curtains make; authentic, remote and judicial describe something else.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Authentic means genuine, the real thing rather than a copy; a stage built from cardboard boxes is the opposite, thrown together from whatever was to hand.
why.C: Remote means far away from everything else, which tells you where a thing is, not what it was pieced together from.
why.D: Judicial means to do with judges and courts of law, which has nothing to do with building a stage.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: After years of training, she finally ______ her goal of qualifying for the finals.
items.explanation: To attain is to reach a goal you have worked for, which is what years of training lead to; to thwart, elude or decline a goal is to end up without it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: Thwarted means stopped or blocked before something could happen; nothing blocked her here, because the years of training paid off and she got there.
why.C: Elude means to slip away from someone, the way a fish eludes your hands, so a goal can slip away from her, but she did not slip away from her goal.
why.D: Decline means to say no to something, or to get weaker over time the way daylight declines; she did not say no to her goal, she reached it.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: News of the accident filled the family with deep ______.
items.explanation: Anguish is severe distress, which is what news of an accident brings a family; clarity, leeway and camaraderie are not kinds of pain.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.B: Clarity means clearness, seeing or understanding something plainly; news of an accident fills a family with pain, not with clear understanding.
why.C: Leeway means spare room or extra time to work in; it is not a feeling at all, and this sentence needs a feeling.
why.D: Camaraderie is the warm friendship between people who spend time together; it is a good feeling, and this sentence needs a painful one.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The principal gave his ______ for the students to leave early.
items.explanation: Consent is permission, which is what a principal gives for students to leave early; a grievance and prestige are not permission, and dissent is disagreement — very nearly the opposite.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A grievance is a complaint you carry about how you have been treated; the principal is allowing the students to go, not complaining.
why.B: Prestige is the respect and high standing a person or place has earned; it is not something you hand to students so they may leave early.
why.C: Dissent means disagreeing with what has been decided, which is close to the opposite of letting the students go.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: The committee could not reach a ______ because several members still disagreed.
items.explanation: A consensus is agreement by the whole group, which is exactly what members who still disagree cannot reach; a refuge, a verdict and a charter are not agreements.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

why.A: A refuge is somewhere you go to be safe from harm; the committee is trying to agree about something, and agreement is not a place.
why.D: A charter is a written paper that sets out what a group may do; the committee is failing to agree, and agreement is not a piece of paper.

items.subject: VR
items.prompt: Scientists tried to ______ the pollution back to its original source.
items.explanation: To trace is to follow something back to where it started, which is what finding the original source means; you cannot cultivate, grant or commend pollution.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE
